items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Gold)
items.title: Gold is not a liquidity hedge: down ~11% YTD into a war-and-deficit backdrop
items.idea: Bullion trades ~$3,830, down nearly 11% this year and on track for its worst year in over a decade, despite geopolitics that 'should' have helped. Jeffrey Currie: 'Gold is a hedge against a solvency crisis down the road. It is never a hedge against liquidity.' Innes reads the market as trading liquidity, real yields and a firm dollar, not distant monetary collapse.
items.angle: Gold falling with equities means it is behaving as a funding asset, not a hedge. The signal to watch is the gold/SPX correlation turning negative again, not any bank's target.
items.tweetA: Gold is down 11% in a year with a war, a Fed hiking again and a chip crash. That isn't a broken hedge, it's the most liquid thing in a margin-call portfolio being sold first. Insurance doesn't pay out while you're still paying the premium. $GLD
items.tweetB: Question for gold bulls: if the solvency-crisis bid never shows up during a 30% NVDA drawdown, when does it? My guess is it only shows up once the Fed blinks. That's a timing trade, not a conviction trade.

charts.desc: 2 charts: gold price path versus forecasts, and gold/equity correlation

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Gold)
items.title: Goldman: $4,650 by end-2027, record $5,600 only in 2028, a 2022-style path first
items.idea: Goldman's Lina Thomas expects 2027 to look like 2022: Fed tightening suppresses private investment demand while central banks provide a structural bid. The leg to the January record (~$5,600) needs Fed cuts and Western ETF inflows to return, which Goldman pushes to 2028.
items.angle: From $3,830, $4,650 is +21% over ~13 months and $5,600 is +46%. The path matters more than the target. Under this sequence, buying aggressively now is a long carry trade against a hiking Fed.
items.tweetA: Goldman's bullish gold call is +21% in 13 months and a new high only in 2028. Translation: you get paid for owning gold after the Fed pivots, and you're early until then. Being early in a hiking cycle costs a lot.
items.tweetB: Everyone will argue about $5,600. The bit that matters is 'resembles 2022'. In 2022 gold went sideways-to-down while real yields ripped. If that's the 2027 template, miners are the pain trade, not the opportunity. $GDX

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Gold)
items.title: Fed at 3.75 to 4% after resuming hikes in September, December hike widely expected
items.idea: Innes notes rates rose to 3.75 to 4% after September's resumption of tightening, with another hike expected in December and sticky inflation pushing expected hikes into 2027. He links higher rates to higher oil prices and says the negative correlation is hurting bullion.
items.angle: A re-tightening Fed while the AI trade unwinds is the macro mix that hurts both long-duration tech and zero-yield gold. That makes cash and short-duration assets the relative winners.
items.tweetA: The Fed is hiking into a 30% drawdown in the market's biggest stock. That's either brave or a policy mistake in slow motion. Either way, real yields are the only chart that matters for both $NVDA multiples and gold.
items.tweetB: Oil up, then rates up, then gold down. The chain that used to be 'inflation is good for gold' now runs through the Fed's reaction function. Hedging inflation with gold only works if the central bank lets inflation run.

items.title: NVDA Q3 FY27: $115.8B revenue (+103%), $130B guide, cloud backlog $2B to $2.5T in 3 months
items.idea: First quarter without Jensen Huang: revenue $115.8B against about $109B expected, data center $107.6B (+110%), and a Q4 guide of $130B ±3% against about $125B consensus, with no China data center revenue assumed. Interim CEO Colette Kress raised FY28 growth to ~75% from 70%. The cloud backlog is $2.5T, up from $2T three months ago, and Vera Rubin did ~$20B in its first quarter of shipments.
items.angle: The backlog grew $500B in a quarter, about 4x NVDA's quarterly revenue, while the stock is -30% in a month. Fundamentals and price are moving in opposite directions, so the fight is now over governance and multiple, not demand.
items.tweetA: Cloud backlog went up $500B in ONE quarter. That's more than four quarters of Nvidia revenue added to the queue, during the worst month for the stock in years. The demand debate is over; this is a governance discount. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia guided $5B above the Street with zero China and an extra week in the quarter. Strip out the extra week and it's roughly 4% sequential growth per week. Still strong, just not the 12% headline people will tweet.

charts.desc: 4 images: earnings summary graphics and AI Tech Wave chart

items.title: NVDA stops China Hopper sales ($2.4B last quarter) despite US approval, and booked $104B via Singapore
items.idea: Nvidia sold ~$2.4B of older Hopper chips to China last quarter and has now stopped, even with US approval; Jensen had been the loudest voice for those sales. The FT reports $104B was booked through Nvidia's Singapore unit last year, almost half the company, after it stopped disclosing Singapore sales. Huang's family worked on the Megaspeed relationship.
items.angle: With Jensen gone, nobody inside Nvidia is pushing for China, and the company is pre-complying before Washington asks. China AI chip self-sufficiency (Huawei, Cambricon) gets a free tailwind.
items.tweetA: Nvidia walked away from $2.4B a quarter in China sales that Washington had already approved. That's not policy. That's a company with no founder left to argue the case. Biggest winner of the Jensen scandal might be Huawei.
items.tweetB: $104B booked through Singapore, about half the company, and they stopped disclosing it. Now Singapore data centers need a license. The China-exposure question for $NVDA was never the $2.4B Hopper line; it was that Singapore number.

items.title: Commerce rule: licences for top chips into Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil from 90 days
items.idea: Data centers abroad must vet customers, and companies based in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil need a license for top chips, effective in 90 days. Nvidia warns it won't sell to customers renting more than half their chips to Chinese companies. DOJ leads a criminal probe of Megaspeed, and Bessent wants answers from the board within ten days.
items.angle: This is the 'remote access' loophole closing. It's a direct hit to SEA neocloud and data center builders (the Johor/Batam corridor) and a relative positive for US-domiciled capacity.
items.tweetA: The new chip rule names Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil and Singapore. Johor was supposed to be the overflow data center capital of Asia. A 90-day licensing clock turns that capex pipeline into a permit queue.
items.tweetB: Nvidia now refuses customers renting more than 50% of chips to Chinese firms. Expect a lot of neoclouds to discover their customer mix is exactly 49%. Enforcement of rules like this lives or dies on KYC, and KYC is where these schemes always break.

items.title: Fed's first-ever AI section in its Financial Stability Report: big banks have ~$1T exposure, 87% of contacts flag AI
items.idea: For the first time the Fed devoted a section of its financial stability report to AI financing. The largest banks have nearly $1T of exposure to the AI build, and 87% of the Fed's market contacts now cite AI as a top risk, up from about half six months ago. Parekh: the '$10T AI build has met its bankers', so it gets built, just slower.
items.angle: When a risk goes from 50% to 87% of survey mentions in six months, it is consensus, not a tail. The likely second-order effect is tighter bank terms for neocloud and data center debt, which ties in with NVDA's own retreat from guarantees.
items.tweetA: 87% of the Fed's market contacts now name AI as a top financial-stability risk, up from ~50% six months ago. Risks that everyone names rarely cause the crash. The one that does is how $1T of bank exposure reprices when the lender of last resort (Nvidia) steps back.
items.tweetB: Same week: the Fed flags ~$1T of bank AI exposure, and Nvidia says its neocloud support will be 'disciplined and selective'. The two biggest backstops of AI capex are both tapping the brakes at once. Watch $CRWV and $NBIS spreads, not their stocks.

items.title: Anthropic IPO: about 7x covered, $10B+ single orders, ~$90B raise, $1.4 to 1.5T valuation, prices tonight
items.idea: Range $70 to $78 (about $1.4T fully diluted), likely pricing in the $80s (about $1.5T) Wednesday night and trading Thursday. The book is close to 7x covered with some single orders above $10B, and the ~$90B including private placement would be the biggest IPO ever, ahead of SpaceX in June. Parekh, ex-Goldman internet research: institutions overbid, hoping to get a quarter or a fifth of what they ask for.
items.angle: Read through Parekh's insider lens, 7x covered with deliberate 4 to 5x overbidding means real demand is perhaps 1.5 to 2x. Still healthy, but a smaller cushion than the headline. Day-one pop risk is higher than durable-demand risk.
items.tweetA: Ex-Goldman IPO veteran says institutions put 4 to 5x what they want in the book. So '7x covered' is closer to 1.5 to 2x real demand. Still good for the biggest IPO ever, just not the frenzy the headline sells.
items.tweetB: $90B raise in a week when Nvidia lost $573B in market cap, the Fed flagged AI financing risk and fund managers made their biggest tech cut in 20 years. If this prices above range anyway, the AI trade isn't dead. It's rotating from picks-and-shovels to the model layer.

items.title: Anthropic compute bill: over $900B of commitments against ~$213B post-IPO cash
items.idea: Per the FT, Anthropic has over $900B of infrastructure commitments over the next two decades and ~$213B of cash after the IPO; the founders call it 'bold but sane'. Parekh has tracked the bill climbing from $517B to $750B to $895B and now over $900B. Amazon and Google will own about 28% between them after the IPO.
items.angle: Cash covers ~24% of commitments. The remaining 76% has to come from revenue growth or future capital raises, so the IPO is the first of many funding events, not the last. AMZN/GOOGL's 28% is roughly $400B+ of marked value at $1.5T.
items.tweetA: Anthropic will have $213B of cash and $900B+ of compute commitments. That's 24 cents on the dollar. The IPO isn't the finish line, it's the first margin call on an AI lab's growth curve.
items.tweetB: Amazon and Google will own ~28% of Anthropic at a ~$1.5T IPO, roughly $420B of value. That's bigger than most of the S&P 500. Nobody is pricing $AMZN or $GOOGL as AI venture portfolios, but that's partly what they've become.

items.title: Cabinet split on Nvidia: Bessent, Rubio and Miller hawks vs Lutnick; Trump reportedly holds up to $62M of NVDA
items.idea: Parekh describes a two-sided game: Treasury Secretary Bessent pushing for answers and backing China hawks alongside Rubio and likely Stephen Miller, against Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who supported chip sales to China and whose sons' firm, Cantor, has data center interests. Trump may hold as much as $62M of Nvidia stock and says he wouldn't mind a Jensen comeback.
items.angle: Policy is being set by a split cabinet, which makes export-control headline risk two-sided and noisy into the Trump/Xi/Putin Shenzhen meeting.
items.tweetA: The President reportedly owns up to $62M of $NVDA, the Commerce Secretary's family has data center exposure, and Treasury is running the investigation. Export policy is now a conflict-of-interest story, and those don't resolve cleanly.
items.tweetB: Which hand wins inside the cabinet decides whether Nvidia's next CEO is a chip guy or a compliance guy. The board just formed a National Security committee. That tells you which way they think the wind blows.

items.title: RAMageddon: memory several times last year's price makes the iPhone Duo a $2,000+ luxury, sold out to Jan
items.idea: Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, is sold out, and mainstream buyers may not get one until December or January. Because memory chips cost several times what they did a year ago, it remains a $2,000+ device. Apple is shipping 'Unlock with Front Camera' (about 0.5s, no depth sensor) in a December update to fix the missing Face ID.
items.angle: Memory inflation is now visible in consumer price points, which is a real-economy signal for the DRAM supercycle. It's bullish for MU and SK hynix margins and a headwind for unit volumes in PCs and phones.
items.tweetA: When a phone launches at $2,000+ partly because RAM costs several times last year's price, the memory cycle has left the data center and reached the checkout counter. That's peak pricing power or demand destruction. Usually it's one, then the other. $MU
items.tweetB: Apple is supply-constrained on its first foldable during the holidays, and the bottleneck is memory, not demand. The AI buildout is literally pricing consumers out of gadgets. Second-order effect of hyperscaler capex nobody models.

items.title: Multi-manager 80:20: 20% of PMs drive 80% of returns, so is diversification hitting a ceiling?
items.idea: Bobby Jain says at highly successful multi-manager platforms only ~20% of PMs drive 80% of returns. Headcount at pod shops has grown with AUM instead of delivering scale economies. Platforms need 8 to 9% net (Ken Griffin) to keep inflows, and they're playing for Sharpe ratio rather than absolute return, which pushes them into ever more strategies.
items.angle: If alpha is that concentrated, more pods add cost and crowding but little return. Crowding risk in pod-shop favourite trades (the factor-neutral AI hardware longs) is the market-relevant angle given the current unwind.
items.tweetA: If 20% of PMs make 80% of the money, the other 80% at a pod shop mostly exist to lower volatility. That's an expensive way to buy Sharpe ratio, and it only works until the crowded trades all de-gross at once.
items.tweetB: Pod shops grew headcount in line with AUM instead of getting scale economies. Combine that with the chip selloff, chips as the 'most crowded trade' and hedge funds crowded into the same AI names, and you have a recipe for synchronized de-grossing.

charts.desc: Charts inside, worth opening (headcount and AUM per employee)

items.title: Citadel ~20% net per year vs Millennium ~14%: the case against the asset-gathering pod model
items.idea: 2026 has been Citadel's year. It has been careful about expansion, while Millennium has become an 'asset gathering machine'. Citadel's long-run net return is ~20% a year versus Millennium's ~14%, though Millennium has lower volatility and better Sharpe ratios. Point72 has expanded with focus, ExodusPoint re-focused on fixed income and Walleye has exited many asset classes.
items.angle: The industry is quietly splitting. Focus (Citadel, Point72) is beating breadth, and second-tier platforms are cutting asset classes. Expect talent-war cost inflation to compress smaller platforms first.
items.tweetA: 6 points a year is the gap between Citadel (~20%) and Millennium (~14%). Compounded over a decade, that's 6.2x vs 3.7x. Millennium sells smoothness; Citadel sells returns. In a year of AI-trade whiplash, smoothness is having its moment.
items.tweetB: Walleye exits asset classes, ExodusPoint goes back to fixed income, Point72 stays focused. Multi-manager platforms are de-diversifying in real time while the marketing still says diversification is the edge.

items.title: Hedge-fund talent wars continue despite 2026 performance wobbles, and Mayfair is the tell
items.idea: Ghose notes no slowdown in senior hiring at multi-manager platforms despite this year's wobbles, and that skill among PMs is 'more unevenly distributed than in most professions', closer to Taylor Swift or Messi economics. The platform pitch is that infrastructure, a central risk book and financing give every seat a leg up.
items.angle: Superstar labour economics at pod shops point to continuing comp inflation for top PMs and pass-through fees, which pressure LP net returns. It's a structural headwind for the industry's 8 to 9% hurdle.
items.tweetA: PM skill is distributed like pop stars, not like accountants. So the pod-shop business is basically a record label: sign a lot of acts, cut fast, and live off the hits. Record labels run on terrible economics for most of their artists.
items.tweetB: Senior hiring hasn't slowed despite a wobbly 2026. When a whole industry keeps paying up for talent during weak returns, the payout keeps rising while the returns don't. Pass-through fees will be the next LP fight.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (BofA FMS)
items.title: BofA FMS (193 managers, $526B): one of the sharpest tech positioning shifts in 20 years, yet no capitulation
items.idea: Hartnett's November survey of 193 participants managing ~$526B (Nov 6 to 12) shows one of the sharpest drops in tech positioning in two decades. Innes's framing: managers are uncomfortable with corporate capex and rotating to defensives and bonds, but haven't cut overall equity exposure. 'Lost their nerve, but not their equity exposure.'
items.angle: Rotation without de-risking is not a bottom signal. The true capitulation marker (cash spike, equity underweight) is still missing, which matches Krinsky's 'another leg lower' call.
items.tweetA: Fund managers dumped tech at the fastest pace in 20 years and kept their overall equity exposure. That's not fear, that's sector rotation. Bottoms come when they sell everything, and they haven't yet.
items.tweetB: The FMS says 'scared of tech, still long stocks'. Pair that with BTIG's 200-DMA warning: if the defensives they rotated into start breaking too, the cash level is the next shoe to drop.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Nvidia lost $2T+ of market cap in weeks (about Turkey's or Spain's GDP), and the +4% AH bounce is 'distinctly underwhelming'
items.idea: NVDA fell more than 30% from its October peak before results. Authers frames the $2T+ loss as roughly the GDP of Turkey or Spain and says a 4% after-hours pop on a beat-and-raise is underwhelming. The valuation on current earnings is 'dirt cheap', but uncertainty stays while the successor is unnamed. Luke Lango: 'They are Jensen's numbers from three months ago.'
items.angle: If the market discounts results as Jensen's legacy, then the real catalyst is the CEO pick, not the next print. That makes Kalshi's CEO market an odd but real hedge instrument.
items.tweetA: Nvidia wiped out a Spain-sized economy in market cap in a few weeks, then beat and raised, and got 4%. When great news buys you 4%, the market is telling you the discount is about who runs the company, not the numbers. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Lango's line is the key: these are Jensen's numbers. Fair enough, but the $2.5T backlog was signed under Jensen too, and it doesn't walk out the door with him. The market is pricing the founder as the moat. I think the moat is CUDA plus supply contracts.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Authers: Huang's return offer 'reeked of entitlement', and Kalshi lists 36 CEO candidates with Huang still 3rd
items.idea: Authers argues affairs with a subordinate and with an important customer suspected of being a Chinese asset are firing offenses that left the board no choice. The board's bigger failure was letting Huang get so powerful. Kalshi offers bets on 36 candidates for Nvidia's next CEO, with Huang still third after the board ruled him out. The Altman 2023 precedent doesn't apply: OpenAI was private and there was no suggestion of wrongdoing.
items.angle: Prediction markets now price CEO succession for a ~$3.7T company, which is a cultural marker of how financialized governance has become. Silicon Valley's petition (180k+ names) versus the board shows a founder-cult governance gap.
items.tweetA: 36 different people you can bet on to be Nvidia's next CEO on Kalshi. The most important succession at the world's #2 company is being priced like the Super Bowl MVP. Succession planning is now a prediction market.
items.tweetB: Silicon Valley's reflex was a petition with 180,000 names; Bloomberg's reflex was 'this reeks of entitlement'. That gap is the whole founder-worship debate in one week. Boards that cave to petitions are why key-man risk gets priced in the first place.

charts.desc: Kalshi odds chart (in the Authers email)

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Gave's Jack Ma parallel: does the Huang affair make the US less investable? The dollar says no, at a ~2-year high
items.idea: Gavekal's Louis-Vincent Gave argues the Huang affair could damage the US as an investment destination, much as the 2020-21 Jack Ma episode made China 'uninvestable', pointing to Chinese perception that Huang is singled out for his descent. His test: if the US looks more attractive, the dollar strengthens and yields fall, and vice versa. Authers: the dollar hit its highest in almost two years last week.
items.angle: It's a clean, falsifiable framework. Use DXY plus 10Y as the market's verdict on US institutional credibility through the Shenzhen summit.
items.tweetA: Gave's test is elegant. If humiliating Jensen makes the US less investable, the dollar falls and yields rise. Instead DXY just hit a two-year high. Markets read it as rule of law, not a Jack Ma moment. For now.
items.tweetB: The Jack Ma comparison misses one thing. Beijing punished Ma for criticising the state; Nvidia's board accepted Huang's resignation over a code-of-conduct breach plus China-linked dealings. Foreign capital can tell the difference, and the dollar suggests it does.

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: 2006 analog: tech underperformed by 16% in Q2 2006, then won by 26% into the GFC
items.idea: BofA's survey shows the biggest shift away from tech in two decades. The last comparable episode, Q2 2006, saw S&P tech underperform the market by 16%, which then became a buying opportunity: tech beat by 26% from July 2006 until the GFC. A record share of managers say companies are overinvesting, and the outlook flipped from 'no landing' back to 'soft landing'.
items.angle: The contrarian setup is there, but the 2006 precedent needed a capex-discipline story to work. NVDA pulling back on financing guarantees might be that catalyst.
items.tweetA: Last time fund managers cut tech this hard was 2006. Tech then outperformed by 26% over the next 18 months. Positioning extremes are not a timing tool, but they're a pretty good map of where the pain trade lives. $XLK
items.tweetB: Record share of FMS respondents say companies are overinvesting, the same week Nvidia says customer financing will be 'selective'. If capex discipline is what investors wanted, they just got it. Be careful what you wish for.

charts.desc: 🔥 FMS tech allocation (biggest cut in 20 yrs) and 'companies overinvesting' record chart

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: End of US exceptionalism? FMS expects non-US to outperform; their S&P 2027 average is 7,926, just 8% up
items.idea: Fund managers now expect non-US equities to beat the US next year. After the internet bubble it took the S&P a decade (from end-2001) to overtake the rest of the world. The weighted average FMS forecast for the S&P 500 at end-2027 is 7,926, just 8% above Tuesday's close and 1.5% above last month's peak. Strategists (Lu Wang's survey) had 7,967 for end-2026.
items.angle: 8% upside over ~13 months is barely above T-bill yields with the Fed at ~4%. That implies an equity risk premium near zero by managers' own forecasts, which is a reason to favour ex-US value and EM.
items.tweetA: Fund managers' own S&P target for end-2027 is +8%. With T-bills paying close to 4%, they're forecasting about 4 points of risk premium for owning the most expensive market in the world. Their allocations haven't caught up with their forecasts. $SPY $EFA
items.tweetB: Post-2001, the S&P needed a decade to catch the rest of the world. The AI cycle is the dot-com cycle's closest rhyme, and managers are quietly positioning for a repeat. America Second might be the 2027 trade.

charts.desc: 🔥 US vs rest-of-world cumulative relative performance since 2001

items.source: Bloomberg Points of Return / John Authers
items.title: Semis still 'most crowded trade' even after MSCI Global Semis fell 36% since June
items.idea: Despite the MSCI Global Semiconductors index falling 36% since June, BofA respondents still label chipmakers the world's most crowded trade. Authers infers they believe the selloff will get much worse. His base case: tech comeuppance, drab US returns and a soft landing, but not a crisis.
items.angle: A trade that is still 'most crowded' after a 36% drawdown hasn't been flushed. Expect relief rallies to be sold until crowding readings fall.
items.tweetA: Semis are down 36% since June and still voted the most crowded trade on Earth. A crowded trade that's already lost a third is where forced selling lives. Bottoms come when the crowd leaves, not when the price falls. $SMH $SOXX
items.tweetB: Nvidia guides to ~$740B of FY28 revenue and semis are still the most crowded trade. Either the crowd hasn't sold because they believe the fundamentals, or they can't sell because they're too big. The answer decides the next 20%.

charts.desc: Most crowded trade chart (in the Authers email)

items.title: NVDA gave back almost all its after-hours gains, and selling spread to sectors that had held up
items.idea: TMAD: the selloff continued Tuesday, with liquidity pulled from sectors that had held up while tech kept weakening. NVDA beat ($115.8B revenue, $2.68 adjusted EPS) but gave back almost all its initial after-hours gains. A weak reaction to good news makes an immediate bounce less likely, so wait for regular-session confirmation. Institutional buying levels are marked on a chart (paywalled).
items.angle: A beat-and-fade on the bellwether when breadth is already broadening to the downside is classic late-stage distribution. It's consistent with Krinsky and the FMS 'no capitulation' read.
items.tweetA: The best possible print from the most important stock, and the after-hours pop already faded. When good news can't hold, the market is telling you who's selling: people who need liquidity, not people who doubt Nvidia. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Selling has moved from tech to the sectors that were holding up. That's the phase where 'rotation' turns into 'de-grossing'. Watch staples and utilities: if they crack, it's no longer about AI.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Tech Breakdown)
items.title: NSA classified network outage ('code yellow') knocked Nasdaq futures, and the cause was a software patch
items.idea: Reports that the NSA's classified internal communications network went down sent Nasdaq futures lower; the incident was rated code yellow, second-highest of three tiers. The WSJ linked it to a software patch, and the NSA confirmed it was routine maintenance with critical systems operational. Apple also had outages across AppleCare, the App Store and Apple Music. Innes: 'A routine software patch can apparently do the job.'
items.angle: When futures trade on unverified outage headlines, the tape is fragile. In this regime, headline risk is asymmetric to the downside.
items.tweetA: A routine software patch at the NSA moved Nasdaq futures. When the market sells on a maintenance window, it isn't pricing risk anymore, it's looking for an excuse. That's the regime to respect.
items.tweetB: Microsoft 365, US banking systems, a nationwide aviation ground stop, the NSA and Apple, all in a few weeks. None of it coordinated, all of it adding up to one theme: 'operational resilience' becomes a line item in tech multiples. Long the boring infra-reliability names.

charts.desc: 2 images: outage tracker and Nasdaq futures reaction

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Tech Breakdown)
items.title: Equinor confirms an ongoing cyberattack, with Europe's gas supply in the frame
items.idea: Norway's Equinor reported an ongoing cyberattack. Innes flags this as the most concerning item, given Equinor's importance to European natural gas supply. Any confirmed compromise of critical operations would warrant far more attention than consumer app outages.
items.angle: Norway is Europe's largest pipeline gas supplier post-2022. A cyber incident at Equinor is a TTF risk premium event even without physical disruption, so watch TTF front-month and Norwegian maintenance and outage notices.
items.tweetA: Equinor, the company that replaced Russian gas for Europe, confirms an ongoing cyberattack, and the headline gets buried under NSA and Apple outages. If you trade TTF, this is the one that matters this week.
items.tweetB: Europe swapped dependence on Russian pipelines for dependence on Norwegian ones. Now the Norwegian operator is under cyberattack. Energy security moved from geography to IT security, and gas prices don't carry that premium yet. $EQNR

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Tech Breakdown)
items.title: FBI FLASH: ARTEX automated pen-test framework gets attackers to privileged access in under 3 hours
items.idea: The FBI warned criminals and state-aligned hackers are exploiting ARTEX, a sophisticated automated penetration-testing framework that takes attacks from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. It's linked to October's ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which exposed Microsoft 365 environments and involved attempted authentication against 2,250+ downstream tenants.
items.angle: AI-driven offence compresses the time defenders have to respond, and that structurally favours autonomous detection and response vendors (CRWD, S, PANW) over human-SOC models.
items.tweetA: Initial targeting to privileged access in under 3 hours, automated. Most enterprise SOCs need longer than that to triage an alert. Attacker dwell time used to be weeks; the defence budget math just changed. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: One supply-chain compromise (ConnectWise), 2,250+ downstream tenants probed. Automated offence scales the way SaaS scales. Security spend has to move from 'more analysts' to 'machine-speed response', and that's a budget shift, not a trend.

items.title: The 'Jensen put': Nvidia did 129 venture deals this year, 27% of global VC deal value, and UBS sees $50B+ at risk
items.idea: Per the WSJ and PitchBook, Nvidia did a record 129 venture deals in 2026, 27% of global VC deal value. UBS estimates a pullback could take $50B or more out of the market. Kress says neocloud support will be 'disciplined and selective', with guarantees starting only once a neocloud has raised its own capital, and some Nvidia-brokered guarantees won't 'exist anymore' if projects are delayed.
items.angle: One corporate investor accounting for over a quarter of global VC deal value is a single point of failure for AI startup funding. Expect down-rounds at GPU-heavy startups and a pivot to sovereign and hyperscaler capital.
items.tweetA: Nvidia was 27% of global VC deal value this year. One company. If its new CFO-turned-CEO pulls back, the AI startup funding market loses a quarter of its oxygen overnight. Rasgon's question is the right one: how much of the AI trade was the Jensen put?
items.tweetB: UBS says $50B+ could come out of AI financing as Nvidia retrenches. Same week, Anthropic raises ~$90B in public markets. Capital is shifting from vendor financing to public equity. Healthier, but the marginal neocloud loses its sugar daddy.

items.title: Nvidia lost $573B in one week (the largest weekly decline for any company on record) and now trails Apple at $3.7T
items.idea: Nvidia's $573B weekly market cap loss last week is the largest for any company on record (WSJ, 'The End of the No-Brainer AI Trade'). At $3.7T it handed the world's most valuable title back to Apple (above $5T). Nasdaq is still well below its October 6 record. It also returned a record $28B in the quarter and added $150B to its buyback.
items.angle: The WSJ calls the AI trade a stock-picker's market now, with hedge funds crowded into the same hardware names. Dispersion trades (long model layer and power, short over-owned hardware) fit that.
items.tweetA: $573B in a week, the biggest weekly loss for any company ever. In the same quarter the company returned $28B to shareholders and raised its buyback by $150B. The company is buying what the market is dumping. One of them is wrong. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Apple back above $5T, Nvidia at $3.7T. A year ago the debate was whether NVDA would hit $10T. The AI trade went from 'no-brainer' to stock-picker's market in six weeks.

items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen Thursday, with chips the stumbling block and Lutnick and Bessent on the plane
items.idea: Trump's third in-person meeting with Xi this year, at APEC in Shenzhen, with Putin present. The WSJ says the Nvidia scandal undercuts Xi's charm offensive and strengthens China hawks in both parties. Commerce's remote-access rule was 'written by and at the direction of' Treasury and the NSC. The Remote Access Security Act and two other chip bills are headed for the year-end defense bill ahead of a Democratic Congress in January.
items.angle: Tight export controls are being written into law before the Congress changes hands, which locks in hawkishness regardless of summit optics. Any summit 'deal' on chips is now constrained by statute.
items.tweetA: Washington writes chip export bills into the defense bill a few weeks before Trump sits with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen. Whatever gets agreed in the room, Congress is making sure the rules outlast the handshake.
items.tweetB: Trump, Xi and Putin in one room in Shenzhen, the city that made China's hardware supply chain. The setting is the message: China wants the chip conversation on its own turf. Watch $TSM and $ASML into Thursday.

items.title: Bessent: Nvidia's next CEO should be an outsider, citing a 'culture of noncompliance'; Wachtell is investigating
items.idea: Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next CEO, citing a 'culture of noncompliance'. The board hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate whether Jensen's conduct compromised national security or Nvidia's secrets. The SEC has a civil probe into whether disclosures misled investors, and Nvidia stopped breaking out Singapore sales last year. Heidrick & Struggles runs the CEO search.
items.angle: A Treasury Secretary publicly steering the CEO pick of a $3.7T company is a new form of state influence over US mega-caps. Expect an 'insider vs outsider' CEO headline as a binary catalyst.
items.tweetA: The US Treasury Secretary is publicly telling a private company's board to hire an outsider CEO. We spent years calling this state capitalism when Beijing did it to Alibaba.
items.tweetB: SEC probe into disclosures, plus Nvidia stopped breaking out Singapore sales the same year Singapore was ~half its revenue. If there's a restatement-type risk at $NVDA, it lives in segment reporting, not in the headline numbers.

items.title: Nvidia's $118B of guarantees: $105B is one OpenAI campus (SB Energy PORTS-Pike, ~4.25 GW, Ohio)
items.idea: Maximum guarantee exposure is $118B, of which $105B is credit support for SB Energy's PORTS-Pike campus in Ohio (~4.25 GW across nine buildings), exclusively hosting NVIDIA infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI. Guarantees phase in from FY29 as buildings come online, and none have been paid to date. The rest: $9.5B power and systems credit support plus $3.5B land, power and shell guarantees for neoclouds.
items.angle: 89% of Nvidia's guarantee exposure is one counterparty (OpenAI) at one site. That's single-name credit concentration, against $53.5B of cash. It's a key credit-risk variable for the NVDA balance sheet that nobody talks about.
items.tweetA: $105B of Nvidia's $118B in guarantees backs ONE campus in Ohio leased to ONE tenant, OpenAI. That's 89% single-name concentration, about 2x Nvidia's cash pile. Nobody calls Nvidia an OpenAI credit proxy, but on this disclosure it partly is. $NVDA
items.tweetB: 4.25 GW for one tenant on 20-year leases, guaranteed by the chip vendor. This is vendor financing on a scale telecom in 1999 would recognise. The difference is the counterparty: Lucent's customers were CLECs, Nvidia's is a lab burning cash to chase AGI.

items.title: GPU rents rising even as token prices fall 60%: Hopper recontracted at up to 2x, B300 rates +60% since launch
items.idea: Management says NVIDIA compute is fully utilized at every hyperscaler and neocloud it serves. Token prices have fallen nearly 60% since May, but cheaper tokens drove more usage, and GPU rental prices are rising across generations: Hopper GPUs recontracted at up to twice their original price on multi-year deals, and B300 rates are up 60%+ since launch.
items.angle: This is direct evidence against the 'GPUs depreciate in 3 years' bear case. If old Hopper re-leases at 2x, neocloud collateral values (and lender recovery assumptions) are better than feared. That's positive for CRWV/NBIS debt.
items.tweetA: Token prices -60% since May. Hopper GPU rents up to 2x on recontract. Output is getting cheaper while the machine that makes it gets dearer. That's Jevons paradox with a balance sheet, and it kills the 'GPUs are worthless after 3 years' short thesis.
items.tweetB: The GPU depreciation bears just lost their best argument: 3-year-old Hopper chips re-leasing at up to double the original rate. If you own neocloud debt, this is the most important line in Nvidia's call. $CRWV $NBIS

items.title: Supply commitments up from $279B to $390B (+$111B in a quarter), mostly multi-year memory
items.idea: Supply commitments rose to $390B from $279B, mainly from multi-year memory procurement. SixSigma ties it to SK hynix's Oct 28 disclosure of long-term agreements covering over 50% of its 2027/2028 capacity. New packaging deals: Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics (substrates) and SPIL (advanced packaging), adding to Amkor, KYEC, Unimicron and IBIDEN. TSMC leadership was in NVIDIA's offices this week.
items.angle: Nvidia's commitments are moving downstream into physical bottlenecks, which locks in memory pricing power through 2028. The substrate names (Kinsus, Unimicron, IBIDEN) are the less-crowded expressions.
items.tweetA: Nvidia added $111B of supply commitments in one quarter, mostly memory, while the stock fell 30%. The company is betting its balance sheet on 2027 to 2028 demand at the same moment investors are betting against it. $MU $000660.KS
items.tweetB: Everyone owns SK hynix for the memory supercycle. The new names on Nvidia's packaging list are Kinsus, SEMCO and SPIL. Substrates are the next bottleneck nobody is crowded in yet.

items.title: Co-packaged optics in volume: Lambda's 10,000+ GB300 deployment; 5x power efficiency, 15x reliability vs pluggables
items.idea: CPO switches are in volume production for scale-out networking. Lambda announced the first production deployment, connecting 10,000+ GB300 GPUs, and NVIDIA claims 5x better power efficiency and 15x higher reliability than pluggable optics. It also announced USFP, a new optical-module form factor, with Cisco. Networking revenue exceeded $21B in the quarter.
items.angle: CPO in volume is the start of a share shift away from standalone transceiver makers (COHR, LITE, InnoLight, Eoptolink) towards switch-silicon owners. Lasers and fiber attach still benefit.
items.tweetA: Co-packaged optics just went from roadmap slide to 10,000-GPU production deployment. 5x power efficiency is the headline, but the trade is who loses the pluggable transceiver socket. $COHR $LITE holders should read the call transcript.
items.tweetB: Nvidia networking did $21B+ in a quarter, bigger than most chip companies' annual revenue. Now it's pulling the optics into the switch package. Nvidia isn't just selling GPUs; it's eating the network bill of materials one layer at a time. $ANET $CSCO

items.title: 1 GW AI factory is about $50B/yr of revenue, so first token one quarter earlier is worth $10B+ (DSX POD)
items.idea: NVIDIA estimates a 1 GW AI factory now generates close to $50B a year of revenue, so reaching first token one quarter earlier is worth more than $10B to the operator. DSX POD, a containerised reference design for Vera Rubin factories validated before delivery, aims to cut deployment from months to weeks. Partners include Dell, Foxconn, Schneider and Vertiv; first pods ship to the US and Central Europe early next year, and European DSX designs nearly eliminate facility cooling water.
items.angle: At $50B/GW/yr, time-to-power is the scarcest input. Modular, pre-validated pods shift value to integrators and power and cooling vendors (VRT, Schneider, DELL) and away from on-site EPC.
items.tweetA: Nvidia says 1 GW of AI factory makes ~$50B a year. The PORTS-Pike campus is 4.25 GW, so about $210B a year of implied revenue from one site in Ohio. Either that number is real and power is the most valuable commodity on Earth, or it's a vendor's marketing math.
items.tweetB: If a quarter's head start is worth $10B per GW, the fastest builder wins, not the cheapest. That's the bull case for prefab: $VRT, Schneider and $DELL selling speed, not hardware.

items.title: Agentic AI drives CPU demand 'far outstripping supply'; Vera CPU revenue to more than double in FY28
items.idea: Kress said agentic AI is driving CPU demand 'far outstripping supply'. CoreWeave, Meta, Nscale and OpenAI have adopted the Vera CPU, joining AWS, Oracle and SpaceX AI, and NVIDIA expects total CPU revenue to more than double in FY28. SixSigma: a tailwind for the CPU category, but more competition for x86 incumbents.
items.angle: Agents are orchestration-heavy (tool calls, branching, memory), which is CPU work. It's a cyclical positive for AMD/INTC server CPU pricing even as Nvidia takes share, plus an Arm royalty tailwind.
items.tweetA: Agents spend most of their time waiting on tools, APIs and memory, and that's CPU work, not GPU. Nvidia now says CPU demand is 'far outstripping supply'. The forgotten chip of the AI trade is back. $AMD $INTC $ARM
items.tweetB: Meta and OpenAI adopting Nvidia's Vera CPU is the quiet headline. x86 isn't losing to Arm in phones anymore, it's losing in the AI data center. Every Vera socket is one less EPYC.

items.title: DSO up from 60 to 64 days on extended terms for 'investment-grade' customers; $109.7B of equity stakes
items.idea: Days sales outstanding rose to 64 from 60, partly due to Rubin shipment timing and partly to extended payment terms on large multi-quarter agreements with certain IG customers. Marketable and private equity investments grew to $44.2B and $65.5B, from $12.9B and $22.3B in January, with another $20B of future equity commitments to frontier labs and infrastructure financiers. Long-term debt is $32.4B, up from $7.5B in January.
items.angle: Equity stakes roughly tripled ($35.2B to $109.7B) in ten months while receivables stretch. Nvidia is increasingly financing its own demand. Watch DSO next quarter: above 70 would be a red flag.
items.tweetA: 4 extra days of DSO on a $130B quarter is ~$5.7B of extra customer credit. Equity stakes tripled from $35B to $110B since January. Debt quadrupled to $32B. Nvidia is quietly becoming the AI economy's bank, and the new CEO says she wants to stop. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia's equity portfolio ($110B) is now bigger than the market cap of most of its customers. When the chip vendor owns your equity, finances your racks and guarantees your lease, 'demand' and 'balance sheet' are the same line item.

items.title: Buybacks over customer financing: $227B authorisation, ~$45B a quarter (2x Q3), 65% of YTD FCF returned
items.idea: Record $28.1B returned in Q3 ($22.1B buybacks, $6.0B dividends), 65% of YTD FCF. $227.3B remains on the authorisation, to be used through FY28, about $45B a quarter, double Q3. Kress ranked shareholder returns 'top priority', ahead of supplier prepayments, committed investments and, selectively, customer financing. Q3 FCF was $43.8B, and FY28 revenue implied at ~$740B.
items.angle: The capital allocation stack flipped: shareholders first, ecosystem last. That supports the stock but removes the 'Jensen put' for neoclouds. Good for NVDA equity, worse for the AI financing complex.
items.tweetA: $45B a quarter of buybacks is more than Nvidia's entire Q3 free cash flow ($43.8B). The new boss just told the market the buyer of last resort for NVDA stock is NVDA, and the buyer of last resort for neoclouds is someone else.
items.tweetB: Kress's ranking: buybacks, then supplier prepayments, then investments, with customer financing last. Under Jensen that list ran the other way. The CFO-CEO is turning a kingmaker into a cash machine. Great for $NVDA, bad for the long tail of GPU clouds.

items.title: ACIE (neoclouds, enterprise, frontier labs' own DCs) now 44% of data center revenue, up from 31%
items.idea: Hyperscale was $60.1B (+71% YoY) and ACIE $47.5B (+195% YoY). ACIE (neoclouds, enterprises and non-hyperscale customers) is now 44% of data center revenue versus 31% a year ago, driven by Rubin shipments to top neoclouds and frontier labs building their own data centers. Rubin did ~$20B in its first quarter, roughly the whole sequential increase, and hyperscalers took Rubin to production in ~1 month, half Grace Blackwell's time.
items.angle: The fastest-growing customer segment is the one Nvidia just said it will finance more selectively, which is the tension in the print. The +195% ACIE growth was partly vendor-financed.
items.tweetA: Non-hyperscaler customers grew 195% YoY and are now 44% of Nvidia's data center sales. These are the customers Nvidia just said it will be 'selective' about financing. The fastest-growing segment is also the most credit-dependent one.
items.tweetB: Frontier labs are now building their own data centers instead of renting from hyperscalers. That's the real shift in the ACIE line: OpenAI and Anthropic becoming their own clouds. Bad news for hyperscaler pricing power on AI, good for Nvidia's customer diversification.

items.title: Gross margin guide 71 to 72% is 'the bottom', from 74.8%, as Nvidia absorbs higher supply costs before repricing
items.idea: Q3 GAAP gross margin was 74.8%. Q4 is guided to 71 to 72% as Nvidia honours existing orders while absorbing higher supply costs (memory) before new pricing takes effect, then 72 to 73% in FY28. Note: since FY27 non-GAAP no longer excludes stock comp. Q3 GAAP net income included a $1.8B private-investment impairment.
items.angle: A ~300bp step-down is memory inflation landing on Nvidia's P&L. If 'everyone pays the same price' and repricing comes in FY28, Nvidia is signalling its own price increase. Pricing power intact, margins temporarily squeezed by suppliers.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's margin is dropping ~300bp because memory makers are taking their cut. When the most powerful chip company on Earth can't fully pass through supplier costs for a quarter, you know who has the leverage right now. $MU
items.tweetB: 'Margins bottom at 71 to 72%, then reprice in FY28' is a polite way of announcing a price hike on Rubin. Customers that have already been squeezed on financing will now pay more per GPU. Watch whether neocloud gross margins can absorb it.

items.title: Druckenmiller at Tomorrow X: setup 'flipped almost 180 since January', capital preservation mode, 'AI washed out, not shorting'
items.idea: SixSigma's notes from the Tomorrow X conference: Druckenmiller says the setup has flipped almost 180 degrees since January, he lacks clarity so has barely any equity exposure (some small positions) but has exposure in other markets, and is in capital-preservation mode. On AI: 'washed out', not shorting it, which implies not long either. Sentiment among AI bulls is poor, with no euphoria.
items.angle: When the best macro trader alive calls AI washed out and still won't buy, that's a liquidity and policy call, not a fundamentals one. It fits with the Fed hiking and gold failing as a hedge.
items.tweetA: Druckenmiller: AI is 'washed out', and he's still not buying. A legend refusing to buy a sector he calls washed out is telling you the problem is the Fed, not the fundamentals. Capital preservation when the Fed hikes is the oldest trade there is.
items.tweetB: Druck 180 degrees from January, mostly out of equities, positioned in other markets. If the best macro trader of the era is sitting this out, the next leg isn't about Nvidia's backlog, it's about rates and the dollar.

items.title: Tomorrow X split: Dell and ALAB CEO say buildout is early; Solomon and Druck say value accrues to the app layer
items.idea: Michael Dell was the most bullish on the AI buildout at Tomorrow X, saying it's early, and the Astera Labs CEO was equally bullish. Lisa Su was pragmatic. Many others, including Goldman's David Solomon and Druckenmiller, leaned towards value going to AI application layers. SixSigma sees heavy groupthink among financial types. Dina Powell McCormick says Zuckerberg's desk at Meta's MSL lab now sits near Alexandr Wang's.
items.angle: The consensus shift to 'apps win, infra loses' is exactly what you'd expect at a sentiment trough. The people selling infrastructure (Dell, ALAB) see order books, while financiers see the stocks.
items.tweetA: At Tomorrow X the people with order books (Dell, Astera) said the buildout is early. The people with portfolios (Solomon, Druck) said value goes to apps. When the sellers of picks and the owners of stock disagree this hard, I trust the order book more. $DELL $ALAB
items.tweetB: 'Value accrues to the app layer' is the new consensus. Same week, Anthropic, a model-layer company, raises ~$90B at $1.5T. If the app layer captures value, why is the market paying $1.5T for the layer underneath it?

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (BTIG Krinsky)
items.title: BTIG's Krinsky, 'Livin' on a Prayer': rallies are for selling, S&P keeps re-testing its 200-DMA
items.idea: BTIG chief technician Jonathan Krinsky says recent recovery attempts look like opportunities to reduce exposure, not a durable bottom. That follows another failed S&P 500 rally and an increasingly uncomfortable test of the 200-day moving average. Deterioration beneath the indices is far more advanced than the headline suggests, software and even defensive tech are showing strain, and 'oversold' alone isn't a reason to buy.
items.angle: Repeated tests of the same support usually weaken it. Combined with a no-capitulation FMS and NVDA fading its beat, the path of least resistance is lower until breadth washes out.
items.tweetA: Every test of the 200-day makes the support weaker, not stronger. The S&P keeps going back to the same line while the average stock is already well below it. The index is the last thing to break, not the first. $SPY
items.tweetB: Krinsky says 'oversold' isn't a buy signal. The BofA survey says managers haven't cut equity exposure. Nvidia can't hold a beat. Put the three together and you get the same answer: no capitulation yet.
